en: The Goddess said:
"O Lord, I have heard everything arising from the Rudrayāmala—
the division of the Trika in its entirety, according to the analysis of the essence within the essence."
Even now, O Supreme Lord, my doubt has not ceased:
what, in reality, O God, is that form which consists of the digits of the mass of sounds?
Or what need is there for the division of the ninefold self within Bhairava, whose form is Bhairava himself?
Is it divided according to the Triśirobhedatantra, or does it consist of the three powers?
Is it composed of *nāda* and *bindu*, or is it the half-moon and the *nirodhikā*;
is it mounted upon the wheels (*cakras*), devoid of vowels (*anacka*), or is it the very nature of *śakti*? (4)
Whether it belongs to the Parāparā, or again to the Aparā,
or even to the Parā— if that were the case, then its status as "Supreme" (Parā) would be contradicted.
For otherness cannot arise through a difference in color or a difference in body; since [the Self] is partless, that [otherness] could not exist even in the state of having parts.
"O Lord, grant me grace; cut away my doubt entirely.
Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent! O beloved, you have asked this very essence of the Tantra."
O blessed lady, although it is most secret and must be concealed, I shall nevertheless tell you everything that has been proclaimed as the complete form of Bhairava.
Therefore, O Goddess, it should be understood as lacking essence, like a magician’s net;
it is indeed comparable to an illusion, a dream, and the delusion of a city of Gandharvas. (9)
For those of deluded intellect who engage in the ostentation of ritual action,
meditation has been described solely for the sake of men whose very selves are destroyed by conceptual construction.
In reality, he is not the ninefold self, nor is he the mass of sounds, nor is he Bhairava; nor is he the three-headed god, nor is he composed of the three powers.
It consists neither of sound nor of the bindu, nor of the half-moon, nor of the nirodhikā;
it is not differentiated by the sequence of the cakras, nor is it of the nature of the Śakti.
For those of unawakened intellect, these are indeed terrifying threats;
everything has been proclaimed for the sake of engagement, like a mother’s sweetmeat. // 13 //
Free from the measurement of space and time, undifferentiated by specific locations or directions, she cannot be designated; in the ultimate sense, she is inexpressible.

That state of the Bhairava-self, which consists of the bliss of internal self-experience, whose sphere of perception is liberated from conceptual construction, and which is full in form—that is Bhairavī. (15)
That form should be known in its true essence as stainless and filling the universe;
in such a supreme reality, who is there to be worshipped, and who is there to be satisfied? (16)
The state of Bhairava that is celebrated in such a manner is the supreme; by virtue of its supreme form, it is proclaimed as the Supreme Goddess (Parā). // 17 //
Just as the non-difference between power and the possessor of power is ever-present, so too, because she possesses those attributes, the Supreme Power belongs to the Supreme Self. (18)
The burning power of fire is not perceived as distinct from it;
this [power] is merely an undertaking for the purpose of entry into the very existence of consciousness. (19)
For one who has entered the state of Śakti, there is meditation without division;
at that time, he becomes identical with Śiva, and this is here called the "Śaiva mouth."
Just as the divisions of the directions and so forth are known by the light of a lamp and by the rays of the sun, even so, O Dear One, Śiva is known through His power.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, marked with the trident and adorned with a skull;
[that which is] void of direction, place, and time, and devoid of designation. 22.
O Bhairava, tell me how I may truly know this: by what means is that state of Bhairava perceived which has a full form, and O Goddess, how does his supreme face come to be? (23)
Bhairava said:
Prāṇa is indeed above and jīva is below; one should utter the supreme [syllable] whose nature is emission.
Because it sustains [all things] in the two places of origin, its state is full.
O Bhairavī, through the non-returning of the pair of voids (viyadyugma), the form of Bhairava is manifested by Bhairavī, whether internally or externally, like the Maruts. 25.
When the power, in the form of the vital breath, has expanded, one should neither go out nor enter;
by means of that [power] in the center through non-conceptuality, there is the state of Bhairava.
When [the breath] is contracted, emitted, or filled, at its conclusion that which is named "Peace" shines forth as peace through its power. // 27 //
Bhairava’s arising consists in contemplating that [light], which shines from its very root like a ray, subtler than the subtlest, fading away at the end of the twelve finger-breadths.
Rising up in the form of lightning, step by step for each wheel,
as far as three fist-lengths above, at the end there is the Great Arising.
The twelve stages correctly differentiated by the twelve syllables— having been liberated again and again through their gross, subtle, and supreme states— are ultimately Śiva.
Having quickly filled [the body] up to the crown of the head by breaking the dam of the eyebrows with a flicker,
and having rendered the mind free from conceptual construction, there arises the emergence of the all-pervading [consciousness] at the very summit of all things.
For one meditating on the fivefold emptiness with mandalas having the variegated forms of peacock feathers, there shall be entry into the heart within the unsurpassed emptiness. (32)
By this very sequence, wherever the contemplation may be—whether upon an empty wall, another vessel, or within oneself—it becomes absorbed and bestows boons. (33)
Placing the mind within the skull and remaining with eyes closed,
one should gradually perceive the supreme object of focus through the stabilization of the mind.
The Lord shines forth by means of that Goddess who resides within the central channel, situated in the middle and having the form of a lotus fiber, meditated upon as the inner void.
When the eye-weapon is restrained by the closing of the eyebrows, blocking the gateway, and the *bindu* is seen to dissolve gradually into its center, there is the supreme state. (36)

For one who meditates on the *bindu*— which has the form of a subtle flame-mole produced by the agitation within the abode— at the end of the crest-lock (*śikhā*), in the heart, and at the end of dissolution, there is absorption (*laya*).
One who is proficient in the Sound-Brahman (śabdabrahman)—which is unstruck, resonant at the ear of the vessel, unbroken in sound, and flowing like a river—attains the Supreme Brahman. (38)

O Bhairavī, by uttering [the mantra] beginning with the Praṇava and ending with the protracted vowel (pluta), through the state of emptiness, one attains emptiness by means of the supreme power (śakti) which is itself empty.
Whosoever of any caste one might cause to experience the two limits [of past and future], that person becomes empty through emptiness and becomes a man whose form is emptiness. (40)
When sounds from stringed instruments and the like are long and established in a sequence,
one whose mind is focused on nothing else will, at the conclusion, become the embodiment of the supreme space.

Through the sequential pronunciation of all the gross phonemes of the *piṇḍa-mantra*, ending with the half-moon (*ardhendu*), the bindu, and the nāda, one becomes Śiva by means of the utterance of the Void (*śūnya*). (42)
One should contemplate space simultaneously in all directions within one's own body;
for one whose mind is free from conceptual construction, everything proceeds as space.
And he who meditates simultaneously on the emptiness of the back and the emptiness of the root shall become empty-minded through a power that is indifferent to the body. (44)
One should meditatively cultivate the emptiness of the back, the emptiness of the base, and the emptiness of the heart with stability;
because of non-conceptuality, they arise simultaneously, and from that, non-conceptuality arises. (45)
One should contemplate emptiness alone within a portion of the body for even a moment;
free from conceptual construction, one becomes free from conceptual construction and partakes in the nature of non-conceptualization.
O fawn-eyed one, one should contemplate all the substances within the body as pervaded by space; then that meditation upon it will become firm. (47)
One should contemplate the division of the skin within another body as being like a wall; by meditating on nothing at all within that, one becomes the object of meditation. 48.
With his senses dissolved in the space of the heart, situated within the hollow of the lotus,
and with a mind focused on nothing else, O fortunate one, he shall attain supreme good fortune.
Through the dissolution of the mind at the *dvādaśānta* from every part of one's own body,
for one whose intellect has become firm, the objective reality of the *tattvas* proceeds as firmly established.
In whatever manner and wherever it may be, one should cast the mind into the dvādaśānta.
For one whose mental fluctuations have been attenuated moment by moment, a transformation will occur within days.
One should contemplate one's own city as being consumed by the fire of time that has arisen from the locus of time; at the end, there will then be the appearance of peace.
In this very way, by meditating with conceptualization upon the entire world as burnt away,
the supreme state of manhood arises for that person whose mind is focused on nothing else.
Having meditated upon the abode of the principles (tattvas), which are increasingly subtle within one's own body or even in the universe, the Supreme (Parā) is manifested at the end.
Having meditated on the power of the pins as weak within the twelvefold field,
and having entered [it] while meditating upon it in the heart, one who is liberated shall attain sovereignty.
One should contemplate everything in its entirety, sequentially in the form of the path of the worlds and so forth,
through the states of gross, subtle, and supreme, until finally there is the dissolution of the mind.
Having meditated upon the Śiva-tattva at the boundaries of this entire universe on all sides, according to the sequence of the paths, one attains great exaltation. (57)
O Great Goddess, one should contemplate this entire universe as having become empty;
and there, the mind itself becomes dissolved, thereby becoming a vessel for that dissolution. (58)
One should cast one's gaze upon a vessel such as a jar, abandoning the wall; having attained absorption in that at that very moment, through that absorption one becomes identical with it. (59)
One should cast one's gaze upon a place such as a treeless mountain or a wall;
when the mental state has dissolved, the exhaustion of mental fluctuations arises.
Having meditated upon the knowledge of both states, one should take recourse in the middle;
and by simultaneously abandoning the two, reality shines forth in the middle.
When mental objects are abandoned and consciousness is stilled, it does not move toward another object;
then, through that intermediate state, meditative cultivation blossoms intensely.
One should contemplate the entire body, or indeed the whole world, as consisting of consciousness;
through a non-conceptual mind, there arises simultaneously the supreme awakening.
Through the friction of the two winds, whether internally, externally, or at their limit, the yogi becomes a vessel for the emergence of the consciousness of equanimity. 64.
One should contemplate the entire world or one's own body as being filled with one's own bliss;
simultaneously, by means of that very nectar of one's own, one becomes composed of supreme bliss. (65)
O gazelle-eyed one, by the practice of guile, great bliss arises immediately, through which reality is revealed. (66)
By binding all the channels, as the vital energy gradually moves upward,
supreme bliss expands at the moment of the touch of an ant.
One should cast the mind, full of bliss, into the midst of fire and poison;
or, being filled solely with air, it is joined with the bliss of Smara.

That bliss of the reality of Brahman which occurs at the conclusion of the immersion into power (śaktyāveśa), stirred by the union with power (śaktisaṃgama), is called the bliss of one's own self. 69.
O Goddess, through the recollection of the fullness of a woman’s pleasure— arising from licking, churning, and striking—
even in the absence of physical power, there occurs an overflowing flood of bliss.
When great joy is attained upon seeing a long-lost kinsman, one should contemplate that arising joy and, becoming absorbed in it, become one-pointed in mind through that dissolution. (71)

Through the unfolding of the bliss of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) arising from the joy produced by eating and drinking, one should contemplate the state of being filled; from that, great bliss (*mahānanda*) arises. (72)

For the yogin whose self is unified with the incomparable bliss of tasting objects such as song and the like, there arises the state of being that very essence through the mind’s ascent into that [bliss]. (73)
Wherever the mind finds satisfaction, one should fix the mind right there;
in each such place, the true nature of supreme bliss manifests.
When sleep has not yet arrived and the external field of perception has vanished,
that state accessible to the mind shines forth as the supreme Goddess.
When the sky is variegated by the light of the sun, lamps, and so forth, one should fix the gaze right there; then one's own essential nature shines forth.
At the moment of being gazed upon by Karaṅkiṇī, Krodhanā, Bhairavī, Lelihānā,
and Khecarī, the attainment of Parā becomes manifest.
On a soft seat, placing one buttock upon it and resting the hands and feet without support, through that practice, the supreme, perfect intelligence shall arise.
Sitting properly on a seat with the arms bent at the elbows and placed in the space beneath the armpits, one brings the mind to tranquility by dissolving it into that [space]. (79)
Having cast a steady gaze upon an object of gross form,
and having rendered the mind supportless in a short time, one shall go to Śiva.
Having placed the consciousness in the middle [of the tongue] while the mouth is wide open and the tongue is in the center,
and uttering the syllable "Ha" with the mind, one then dissolves into the state of peace.
Remaining on a seat or in a reclining posture, one should contemplate one's own body as being without support; when the mind is thus dissolved, one becomes instantly free from all latent tendencies.
Then, O Goddess, for one who remains on a steady seat, either by gradually moving the body or when the state of the mind has become tranquil, one shall attain the Divine Current (divyaugha). 83.
Beholding the stainless sky with an uninterrupted gaze, O Goddess, one whose self is steadfast shall in that very instant attain the form of Bhairava. (84)
One should contemplate everything dissolved in the sky at the crown of the head as being Bhairava;
one should then enter into that reality of the splendor of Bhairava’s form which pervades all of it. (85)
Whatever little is known gives rise to duality, whereas external light is darkness;
yet, having realized the form of Bhairava as the universe and all else, one becomes the bearer of infinite light.
In this very way, when the dark fortnight has long arrived during the terrible night,
he will come assuming a form shrouded in darkness, a form that is terrifying.
In this very way, first closing one's eyes and then opening them, one should visualize the form of Bhairava appearing black before oneself; by contemplating it, one becomes absorbed in that.
Furthermore, through the impairment or cessation of any sense faculty whatsoever, when one has entered into the non-dual void, the self is manifested right there. (89)
O Goddess, for one who recites the letter *a* without the nasal dot (*bindu*) or the visarga, the great flood of knowledge, the Supreme Lord himself, suddenly arises. (90)
Meditate upon the consciousness that ends with the *visarga* of the vowel along with its *visarga*;
through a mind free of support, one should touch the eternal Brahman. 91.
One should meditate upon one's own self as having the form of the sky, unenveloped by the directions;
then the supportless power of consciousness reveals its true nature.
Having first pierced some part of the body with a sharp needle or similar instrument,
and having then yoked consciousness to that very spot, there is a stainless state in Bhairava.
There is no internal mental construction such as "I shall meditate" within me;
through the absence of conceptual constructions, one becomes liberated from conceptualizations. // 94 //
Māyā is called "the deluder"; the manifestation of the *kalās* is established.
By discerning such characteristics of the *tattvas*, one should not become separate [from them]. (95)
Upon perceiving a desire that has suddenly arisen, one should bring it to rest;
for it dissolves back into that very source from which it emerged. (96)
When neither desire nor knowledge has arisen in me, who indeed am I then?
In reality, one should become such as that, absorbed in that, and with the mind fixed on that.

When desire or knowledge has arisen, one should fix the mind [upon it] with the thought "this is the self," with an undistracted mind; from that comes the vision of the reality of things as they are. 98.
"O Dear One, knowledge would then be signless, without support, and illusory in nature; in reality, nothing whatsoever exists in such a state—Śiva alone does. (99)
The nature of consciousness exists in all bodies; there is no distinction anywhere.
Therefore, a person who has conquered existence should contemplate everything as being composed of that [consciousness]. 100.
Having rendered the intellect motionless within the sphere of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy, that Reality alone remains. 101.

For one who meditates upon the entire universe as consisting of a magical illusion—whether as something dispersed like a painted scene, or as something whirling—the arising of happiness occurs for both the one who contemplates it and the one who perceives it. (102)
One should not cast the mind into suffering, nor should one cast it into pleasure;
O Bhairavī, let it be known that in the middle, what reality remains? 103.

Having abandoned the notion that [the self] resides within one's own body, and contemplating with a firm mind and vision that "I am everywhere," one should become happy, not looking for anything else. 104.

Furthermore, when one meditates that the cognition or the desire and so forth within oneself regarding a jar or other objects has not arisen as being omnipresent, [the yogi] becomes all-pervading. (105)
The cognition of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject is common to all embodied beings;
however, for yogins, there is a distinction: they possess attentiveness regarding the relationship [between them]. (106)
One should experience consciousness even in another body as if it were one's own;
by abandoning attachment to one's own body, one becomes all-pervading within days.
Having rendered the mind supportless, one should not conceptualize further conceptualizations;
O deer-eyed one, that is the state of both the individual self and the supreme self—Bhairava.
"The Supreme Lord is omniscient, the creator of all, and all-pervading; I am He alone, a follower of the Śaiva dharma"—through such firm conviction, one becomes Śiva. (109)
Just as waves belong to water, the flickering flames to fire, and the radiance to the sun,
so too these various manifestations of the universe are merely differentiated forms of myself, Bhairava.
Through repeatedly wandering with the body and then swiftly falling to the ground,
the state of Parā arises upon the cessation of the power of agitation.
Alternatively, due to incapacity regarding the supports, or through ignorance, or by the dissolution of the mind,
at the conclusion of the agitation caused by the descent of power (śakti-samāveśa), one's form becomes Bhairava.
O Goddess, listen to this tradition; I shall explain it correctly to you:
liberation arises immediately when the two eyes are merely fixed in a steady gaze. (113)
Having contracted the ears and likewise the lower opening,
while meditating on that which is without vowels and without consonants, one should enter the eternal Brahman.
By standing in a great pit such as a well and gazing upward, the dissolution of the mind occurs clearly and immediately for one whose intellect is free from conceptual construction. (115)
Wherever the mind goes, whether externally or internally, there alone is the state of Śiva; since he is all-pervasive, where can it go?
Wherever the consciousness of the All-pervasive Lord is manifested through the path of the senses,
because that [consciousness] has those [senses] as its sole substrate, it attains a state of fullness through absorption into Cit.
At the end of hunger and other such states, in fear, in grief, in a deep abyss, or when fleeing from battle;
likewise at the end of curiosity or hunger—therein lies the state consisting of the reality of Brahman.
While objects are being recollected, one should cast the mind toward the place where they were seen;
having rendered one's own body supportless, the Lord [of the mind] flows forth.
Having fixed one's gaze slowly upon some object, one should withdraw it;
that knowledge, together with the mind, O Goddess, becomes the absorption in emptiness. //120//

The kind of consciousness that arises in one who is detached due to the intensity of devotion—that is the power of Śaṅkara; therefore, one should constantly cultivate it, for through that, one becomes Śiva.
When another object is being cognized, emptiness resides in all things;
having meditated upon that very [emptiness] with the mind, one becomes tranquil even while [the object] is known. 122.
That purity which is taught by those who know only a little is not true purity in the vision of Śambhu;
for one is neither pure nor impure. Therefore, one should become happy through being free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa). 123.
The state of Bhairava is everywhere, even within common objects;
since there is nothing else apart from that, the realization is non-dual. (124)
He is the same toward enemy and friend, and the same in honor and dishonor.
Knowing that Brahman is all-pervasive, one should become happy. // 125 //
One should never cultivate hatred anywhere, nor should one ever cultivate passion;
liberated from both passion and hatred, one moves toward Brahman in the middle. 126.

That which is unknowable, that which is ungraspable, that which is empty, and that which has reached non-existence—all that should be contemplated as Bhairava; at its end, the arising of awakening occurs.
Having fixed the mind upon the external space— which is eternal, supportless, empty, all-pervading, and devoid of conceptualization— one should enter the spaceless state.
Wherever the mind goes, at that very moment and by that very means, one should abandon it through non-abiding; thus, one becomes waveless. // 129 //
"Because he causes everything to resound out of fear, he is the giver of all and pervades the entire universe"; thus, through the continuous utterance of the word *bhairava*, one becomes Śiva. (130)
Due to the cessation of such notions as "I" and "this is mine," the mind,
being without a basis, becomes tranquil through the impelling force of that meditation.
Eternal, omnipresent, without support, all-pervading, and the sovereign of all, he meditates upon sounds at every moment and has achieved his purpose in accordance with their meaning. (132)
"All this that exists is unreal, appearing like a magical illusion.
What is the reality behind a magical illusion?"—by holding fast to this thought, one should attain tranquility. (133)
Where is there knowledge or action for the self, which is changeless?
Since external objects depend upon knowledge, this world is therefore empty.
For me there is neither bondage nor liberation; these are merely terrors for one who is afraid.
This is a reflection of the intellect, like that of the sun in waters. (135)
All encounter with pleasure, pain, and so forth is mediated by the senses;
thus, having renounced the senses, one remains established in oneself, abiding in the Self. (136)
Everything that illuminates is knowledge, and the Self is the illuminator of all; because it is a single entity with a single nature, knowledge and the object of knowledge are discerned as one. (137)
When the quartet consisting of the mind, volition, power, and the self is completely dissolved into the Beloved, then that is the form of Bhairava. (138)
O Goddess, one hundred and twelve instructions on the waveless state have been taught in brief; by knowing which, a person becomes a knower of wisdom. (139)
And here, one who is disciplined in even a single [practice] becomes Bhairava himself;
through speech, he performs actions, bestowing both curses and favors.
Endowed with the powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest, he attains freedom from old age and death;
O Goddess, he is beloved by the yoginīs and is the lord of all melāpakas. 141.
"Even while living, he is liberated; even while acting, he is not defiled.
Śrī Devī said: "O Lord, O Maheśvara, if this body belongs to the Supreme Goddess... (142)
When such a state has been thus established, who recites and what is the recitation?
O Great Lord, who meditates, who is worshipped, and who is satisfied? (143)
"To whom does the invocation belong? To whom does the fire-oblation (homa) belong? And what is sacrifice (yāga), and how is it performed? Śrī Bhairava said:
"O fawn-eyed one, this external procedure pertains only to those who are still coarse [in their perception]. (144)
That meditation which is cultivated again and again within the supreme state is itself the recitation; here, the sound whose essence is mantra is the object of such recitation. (145)
For meditation is indeed unwavering awareness, formless and without support;
meditation is not the conceptualization of a body, eyes, face, hands, and so forth. 146.
What is called "worship" is not merely that firm mental resolve made with flowers and other offerings;
rather, worship is indeed the dissolution with devotion into the non-conceptual great void.
In this context, that state which arises day after day while established in any one of these methods—
the state of being full in form— is here called "satisfaction," which is absolute plenitude.

In the fire that is the abode of great emptiness, the elements, the sense faculties, the objects, and so forth, are offered together with the mind; this is the oblation performed with the ladle of consciousness. (149)
O Supreme Goddess, sacrifice here is satisfaction characterized by bliss; it is called *yāga* because it destroys all sins and protects everything, O Pārvatī. (150)
The immersion into the power of Rudra is that supreme field of contemplation;
otherwise, what worship could there be for that reality, and who would be satisfied? (151)
For one's own self is everywhere essentially nothing but autonomous bliss and pure consciousness;
immersion into that very nature is declared to be the bath of one's own self. 152.
Whatever substances are used for worship or for satisfying the Supreme and the Non-Supreme, and whoever is the worshiper—all that is but one; where, then, is the act of worship? (153)
The vital breath may depart and the individual soul, crooked in form, may enter by its own will;
she is the long-souled Great Goddess, the supreme and non-supreme one in the field of another. 154.
Standing in attendance at this sacrifice consisting of great bliss, one who is entered by that Goddess shall attain the supreme Bhairava. 155.
Twenty-one thousand six hundred recitations of the Goddess are prescribed; they are easily obtained by the wise, but difficult for the dull-witted to attain. (156)
Thus, O Goddess, this supreme and most excellent nectar has been declared; and this must never be revealed to anyone at any time. 157.
[This is forbidden] toward the disciple of another, the wicked, the cruel, and those who lack devotion at the feet of the Guru;
however, [it is permitted] for heroes of elevated soul whose minds are free from conceptual construction. 158.
One should give without hesitation to the devotees and the circle of gurus a village, a kingdom, a city, a country, or one's sons, wife, and family. (159)
"O fawn-eyed one, having abandoned all this, you must accept this:
O Goddess, what use are these unstable things? This supreme wealth is stable.
Even one's life-breaths may be given away, but the supreme nectar must not be given. (160)
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Śaṅkara, I am fully satisfied;
today I have grasped the essence of the Rudrayāmala Tantra.
"Today the heart of all the various powers has been known," having said this, the goddess, filled with bliss, clung to Śiva's neck.
